title: Disney to lay off at least 100 workers in theme parks division
summary:
Disney is laying off between 100 and 200 workers across its theme parks division as the entertainment giant continues a restructuring programme.

The job cuts were confirmed by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorised to comment publicly, the Los Angeles Times reports.

The layoffs are limited to Disney Experiences and are part of an evaluation of the segment's priorities, investments and project timelines, the person said.

The cuts are the latest in a series of reorganisations at Disney under new CEO Josh D'Amaro, who took over the role in March, succeeding Bob Iger.

Part of Disneyland Resort in California, Disneyland opened as the first Disney theme park in July 1955 Disney

The Walt Disney Company recently laid off nearly 300 workers and offered early retirement packages to older employees.

At Bloomberg News' Screentime media conference in Hollywood on 1 October, Disney's president Dana Walden said: "There is a need to constantly evaluate how you’re structured.

"It is extremely painful. We’ve exited colleagues who I’ve worked with for most of my career and it is, in many ways, a harsh reality."

In April, D'Amaro announced the elimination of around 1,000 positions at Disney as the company works to "streamline our operations".

Growth at Disney parks

In its most recent earnings report, Disney's theme parks division reported a 10 per cent rise in revenue, as well as operating income growth of 20 per cent.

Attendance rose by 4 per cent year-over-year at Disney's global attractions, with particular strength at Walt Disney World and additional capacity at Disney Cruise Line.

D'Amaro said the company is "proud of the growth that we’ve had this year, and we’re investing to sustain that growth".

“The pipeline includes major attractions at every site, including Villains Land in Orlando and the Avengers Campus expansion in Anaheim, amongst others in the US, and our previously announced cruise ship expansion,” he added.

title: Maurer Rides introduces the Spike PM360 transportainment system
summary:
Maurer Rides, a leading designer and manufacturer of roller coasters and transport solutions, has launched the Spike PM360, an electrically powered passenger transport system that offers both movement and entertainment.

The system features a pivot-mounted cabin that stays level through horizontal, overhead, steep, and vertical track sections, keeping passengers seated upright throughout the journey.

This unlocks new opportunities for transport connections and standalone attractions, such as resort shuttles and rideable landmarks.

Project inquiries for the PM360 are now open.

PM360 Mountain Railway - Concept rendering. AI-enhanced visualization.© Maurer Rides

New opportunities, proven technology

A rail-guided passenger transport system, the PM360 boasts a cabin with a 360 degree pivoting suspension that allows for any track angle.

This is paired with the company's tested Spike rack-and-pinion technology, which delivers complete, positive transmission of drive force in any position, irrespective of gradient, weather conditions or load. As such, the PM360 can handle steep gradients and vertical sections that exceed the capabilities of traditional passenger transport systems.

Each vehicle has its own drive and braking system, meaning no additional components are required along the track, streamlining infrastructure and maintenance. The electric drive is also quiet, produces no local emissions, and recovers energy during braking.

Maurer Rides has coined the term 'transportainment' to describe a blend of passenger transportation and entertainment.

By bringing its roller coaster engineering expertise to new transport applications, the company is crafting journeys that not only connect destinations, but provide an experience in their own right.

Potential uses include shuttle connections within resorts, experience-oriented routes in urban areas, and standalone attractions that leverage the flexible track layout. This can be used to create dramatic structures, turning the track itself into an architectural landmark.

PM360 Vertikal - Concept rendering. AI-enhanced visualization.© Maurer Rides

Jörg Beutler, CEO, Maurer Rides GmbH, says: "Operators often face the challenge of connecting areas at different elevations, with limited space and high architectural design requirements.

"With the Spike PM360, we open up new possibilities: the track can even run vertically while passengers remain seated upright. This allows a transport connection to become a standalone attraction in its own right."

As with all Spike products, the PM360 is based on the modular Spike platform which drives Maurer Rides' roller coasters. This year, Spike is presented across the company's full range of applications, positioning transportainment as part of an integrated system ranging from amusement parks to urban environments.

Recently, Maurer Rides announced two further additions to the Spike series, Spike Train and Spike Tandem.

title: WhiteWater’s Vantage: Why attraction technology must evolve beyond launch
summary:
WhiteWater’s Vantage platform, a next-generation visitor engagement and technology unification solution, is now deployed at 12 visitor attractions across the US.

The rollout marks one of the most ambitious guest technology integrations in the attractions business, connecting ticketing, payments, loyalty, food and beverage, retail, access control and mobile engagement into a single ecosystem designed around the guest.

But what happens once a visitor attraction has invested in a new technology? How does it adapt to the needs of frontline employees, evolve alongside the operations, and continue delivering value long after launch?

Blooloop speaks to Charlie Hill, head of product at Vantage, and Lucas Appratto, customer success manager at Vantage, about the people using the platform every day, how the technology can evolve over time, and why an ongoing partnership between an operator and its technology provider is key to long-term success.

Charlie Hill, head of product at Vantage, and Lucas Appratto, customer success manager at Vantage

For Appratto and Hill, ensuring the platform works for the people using it every day is a crucial part of the process. That means listening closely to frontline employees – the people who interact directly with guests and rely on the systems throughout the day.

In early 2026, EPR acquired seven Six Flags properties, with Enchanted Parks operating the six US sites, which are: Valleyfair (Minneapolis, Minnesota), Worlds of Fun (Kansas City, Missouri), Michigan’s Adventure (Grand Rapids), Schlitterbahn Waterpark Galveston (Texas), Six Flags St. Louis (Missouri), and Six Flags Great Escape (Queensbury, New York).

The Vantage system is powering each park’s operations.

Combined, the above theme parks welcomed around 4.5 million visitors for the full year ended 31 December 2025, generating approximately $260m in net revenue.

Listening to frontline staff

“A lot of it comes down to speed. One extra tap on a screen is never going to show up on a dashboard; leadership wouldn’t look at it. But multiply it by 1,000 guests in front of you on a hot Saturday, and suddenly there’s a long line right in front of you. The staff notice the little things,” Appratto says.

“We actually had a case where tapping cancel on one screen undid the guest’s redemption, and so they didn’t count towards attendance. It was the gate teams who flagged it; a simple, easy mistake to make that affects a bigger process inside of the park.”

He adds: “I’ve been the person at the gate with a line in front of me. When a site tells me something isn’t working, I actually get it, and I feel the anxiety that they feel.”

WhiteWater's Vantage: Why launching new technology is just the beginning WhiteWater

One example comes from Appratto’s tenure as a frontline employee at Island H2O Water Park in Florida, which integrated the Vantage platform in 2019. At the time, the water park encountered an issue with processing annual passes, which resulted in long queues and a frustrating experience for guests.

Appratto was part of the marketing team, but due to the long lines at the site, he was assisting guest services with processing season passes.

“At the beginning of each season or as a specific sale went live, we would have thousands of people who wanted to get their benefits or cards, and we would have lines out into the parking lot," he says.

Recognising the need for an improved approach, Appratto proposed a digital solution that would streamline pass processing and improve the guest experience.

Improving the guest experience

“It needed to be fixed because the experience for the guests was horrible, so I brought a solution to the team, first at the park, and asked if we could process annual passes digitally,” he says.

“We had Vantage technology at the site, and I called up Aaron [Mendelson, Vantage senior vice president], who is now my boss. I told him about the issue and how it was affecting the visitor experience, and how it might be a good segue into getting people to download the app and start getting engaged with the technology in the park before they even get there.”

Guests use a mobile app, part digital assistant and part wallet, to interact with attractions powered by Vantage.

Technologies in the platform for visitors include fast, tokenised cashless transactions; in-app purchasing to add upgrades, merchandise and experiences straight from a phone; and a gamified loyalty layer that rewards them for exploring and engaging.

“Aaron went away and talked to the ticketing partners, and then they developed the solution to be able to virtually process guest passes, which eliminated the lines for pass processing at the front gate once we rolled it out,” says Appratto.

After launch

“Typically, we go into hypercare mode once we’ve got the technology live at the client site. We watch and make sure that it’s working exactly the way that it’s supposed to,” Hill tells us.

“We can do all the research on the front end that we possibly can, but when we get the product into a user’s hands, it may not work the way that they need it to. We go into a phase called rapid response engineering.

"We address concerns as fast as we possibly can, and stay in the loop until we’ve got it working the way that it needs to.”

Appratto says: “Ultimately, launch day isn't the finish line. It's really just the beginning of the relationship between the operator and us, the technology. Testing tells us if the system works. Opening day tells us if it works with the line at the door and hundreds of people right in front of us.”

Guests use a mobile app, part digital assistant and part wallet, to interact with attractions powered by VantageWhiteWater

Solid communication, Hill says, is part of a healthy relationship between an attraction and its technology partner once the product is up and running.

“It sounds so trite, but it’s about really solid communication and direct lines of communication to the people who can make decisions. A lot of the time, the people who can authorise a decision are different to the people who are experiencing the pain or benefits of a decision,” he adds.

“What we try to do is make sure that we have an ongoing relationship with the theme park, and make sure that there’s a voice at the table who understands what it’s really like to use the tool, who might be experiencing pain points or benefits, or asking for a feature.”

Communication and collaboration

Hill says: “We make sure that everyone is involved and aligned to the same goal. Not every operator wants to run their sites the same way. Some companies are really operator-minded, and some are obsessed with the guest experience and want to talk about the operations later.”

Collaboration and transparency are key, according to Hill and Appratto.

Hill says: “As long as there is a tremendous amount of collaboration between the theme park operations and our company across different levels, we can build the tools that will optimise for the goals that they want to achieve.”

Appratto adds:

“To me, a healthy relationship is one with no surprises in either direction, where the customer feels comfortable telling us early on when something isn't working, and where we are honest about what we can fix now versus what can be a bigger change down the road. As long as there's transparency, that's what a healthy relationship looks like.”

In early 2026, EPR acquired seven Six Flags properties, including Worlds of Fun in Kansas City, Missouri EPR

From a wider product development perspective, “the absolute best feedback about how something should work comes from the people who use that software every day”, Hill says.

“You may have spent 30 years in product development, but then you’ve got a 16-year-old running admissions and having a hard time with some particular flow. Everyone’s voice matters very much, and we will take the time to listen to you,” he adds.

“The faster you can take that feedback from those frontline folks and iterate it into a great product, or get it out there and test, test, test, the quicker you get to the best solution in the situation.”

An evolving product

The product should ideally evolve as an attraction and its operations change and grow, Hill says:

“It’s really important that you don’t build and design in a way that you’re rigid to the way that the product worked yesterday, and that you anticipate that priorities, processes and desires are going to change.”

Additionally, building a platform that can serve different attractions means striking a balance between responding to the specific needs of an individual site and creating technology that can evolve across the wider industry. The platform, Hill says, “has to work for everybody”.

“If we build something that’s overfit to one use case, then sometimes that’s not going to scale out well to others. The very first thing we do once we get a requirement is start thinking about the general principles behind what the operator wants to achieve.

"Sometimes an operator will describe what they want in a really specific way, and we have to take that apart and look at the pieces,” he adds.

Enchanted Parks has selected the Vantage platform as its visitor engagement and technology unification solution WhiteWater

That does not mean asking operators to change the way they run their attractions to fit the technology, as Vantage aims to remain open to different approaches.

“If somebody wants to do something differently, we do not say, ‘No, we’re not going to do that.’ We’re very respectful of the following principle, which is that we want to help operators run their parks the way that they want to run their parks. The principle of being open minded really matters,” Hill says.

He adds:

“What we've learned from working with operators that we wouldn't learn from development in isolation is that not every principle applies equally in all contexts, and the absolute best thing to do is to go sit with the operator, watch what's happening, listen to them, and when they say something, particularly when it it runs against what you already believe, is just say, ‘I trust you and I'm going to put a lot of stock into that.’”

Trends in the attractions business

Hill predicts that integrating every touchpoint of the visitor journey will become increasingly important to the theme park and attractions industry. “It’s going to matter more and more over time,” he says.

At Enchanted Parks, for example, the Vantage ecosystem includes TicketSpice for ticketing and distribution, VersioPay for omni-channel payments, Zucchetti's TC POS for food, beverage and retail, and Lodgical for resort operations.

Each was chosen for its strength in its own domain, with Vantage unifying them into a single guest record.

EPR has acquired seven Six Flags properties, with Enchanted Parks to operate the six US sites EPR

“We think there will only be more collaboration between vendors in the future. There will only be more specialists wanting to participate in things,” Hill adds.

“We're betting and observing that the companies that are the absolute best at what they do will continue to stand out and innovate in their particular lanes. But they may not become generalists across the space, so they will always need great integration partners who are going to be there to help tie everything together and make it work the way that it's supposed to.”

title: ​Bringing nature and play together at visitor attractions
summary:
A woodland area that might otherwise sit at the edge of a visitor attraction can become a destination in its own right. Elevated walkways, suspended bridges, timber towers, and places to stop and explore can encourage families to discover their surroundings from a different perspective,

At the Bronx Zoo, Nature Trek brings this idea to life.

Opened in 2017 through a collaboration between the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) and SimEx-Iwerks, the attraction weaves elevated pathways, towers and bridges through a wooded area, creating what Sean McAllister, senior vice president at SimEx-Iwerks, describes as a “village in the trees.”


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bronx Zoo (@bronxzoo)

The attraction welcomes around 500,000 guests a year. Its appeal lies not just in the structures themselves, but in the journey between them: visitors can explore at their own pace, discover different features along the way, and share the experience across generations.

For zoos, safari parks, botanical gardens and other outdoor attractions, this approach offers another way to make the most of existing landscapes.

SimEx-Iwerks’ Nature Attractions portfolio encompasses elevated trails, canopy walks, net-based play and natural playgrounds, with designs tailored to each site’s surroundings and operational requirements.

​Outdoor adventures to reach a broader audience


Unlike traditional ropes courses, SimEx-Iwerks' Nature Attractions do not require visitors to wear harnesses, making them an alternative for operators looking to offer outdoor adventure to a broader range of guests.

The design is intended to let families explore together, with routes and challenges tailored to the site. Accessible routes can be incorporated.


"The shared family experience is very appealing," McAllister adds. "We want adults to participate alongside the kids."

Operationally, the harness-free model reduces labour needs. Unlike systems that require large crews of certified technicians, safety monitors, and rescue-trained operators, nature treks need minimal supervision, lowering daily costs while maintaining throughput.

"The biggest misconception is that we’re proposing another ropes course," says McAllister. "Operators may immediately think about harnesses, specialist staffing, waivers, and an experience that only some of their guests will want or be able to do.

“Our Nature Trek and canopy trail designs take a different approach. The experiences are designed for families to enjoy together.

“This really changes the conversation.”

​Four approaches to nature-based play


SimEx-Iwerks' Nature Attractions portfolio comprises four products, each custom-designed to suit the site's landscape, vegetation and intended visitor experience.

Nature Trek combines elevated trails, timber towers, suspended bridges and netted tunnels to create a route through the trees. Typically positioned 10-15 feet above the ground, it balances active challenges with places to pause and take in the surroundings.


Accessible routes can be incorporated where the site and layout permit.

Canopy Walk focuses on elevated viewpoints and the surrounding landscape. Usually 15–20 feet above ground, its suspended bridges and treetop platforms offer new perspectives on woodland, planting, and nearby habitats.

Optional lighting, audio and interpretive elements can extend its use beyond daytime visits.

title: ​Ectovox on the changing role of storytelling in water parks
summary:
Water parks are becoming more than collections of slides and pools. As guest expectations evolve, operators are creating destinations that combine aquatic attractions with storytelling, theming and immersive experiences.

That shift is changing design's role in water park development. For Ectovox, the answer is to bring creative development and engineering together from the outset, combining narrative, visual design and planning with the technical expertise needed to deliver complex aquatic environments.

Based in Orlando, Ectovox grew out of Martin Aquatic’s concept studio and became its own experiential design division. It works across water parks, resort amenities, cruise and other location-based entertainment projects.


Ectovox’s multidisciplinary team includes storytellers, graphic artists, 3D modellers and interior designers alongside aquatic engineers and master planners.

Its projects range from cruise destinations and expansions to indoor water parks built around established brands, including Mattel and Hasbro. The goal is to develop aquatic destinations as complete experiences, considering the creative concept and physical environment together.

​From Martin Aquatic to Ectovox


In 2019, Martin Aquatic’s in-house creative team led a corporate rebrand and created the Martin Aquatic identity. The work attracted attention from developers and others in the industry, who began asking who was behind it.

The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 disrupted development schedules across the industry, but it also let the company explore how its creative team could support clients beyond traditional aquatic design and engineering.


As demand grew for branding, digital artwork, and marketing, the creative team became a more formal offering and eventually became Ectovox, a division focused on experiential design, storytelling, and master planning.

An early collaboration with themed entertainment specialist Chris Grap, now VP of Ectovox at Martin Aquatic, helped shape the direction. At the time, Grap was vice president of experiential development at Mall of America and was working with the team on Mystery Cove.

“Chris was both a client and a friend working with Mall of America at the time on Mystery Cove, and we got a really good flavour of our ability to work together,” says Josh Martin, president and creative director at Martin Aquatic.


“That led us to go, 'Hey, we'd like to do more of this work.' Now our focus has largely been on taking these destinations and creating the full experiential design. It really goes back to storytelling.”

Grap says the new division gave the work a clearer identity and allowed the team to pursue a wider range of projects.

"When you hear Martin Aquatic, that is broad, but it's limiting in the sense of when you start to think about experiential design and guest experience. The team had been doing this work but really wasn't getting credit or recognition for it.

“What I think Ectovox does is allow for a wider scope that branches a bit more outside what you would have expected from Martin Aquatic, and it's been interesting to see the opportunities that have come our way from it.”

​Bringing creative design and engineering together


Ectovox brings market research, master planning and creative development together from the beginning of a project.

An in-house team of market researchers conducts competitor and feasibility benchmarking; Martin leads designers focused on master planning, spatial layout, and operational flow, while Grap focuses on thematic narrative and character development.

The team includes mechanical engineers, interior designers, former show-set construction specialists, graphic artists, 3D animators and computational fluid dynamics experts. This allows the team to consider creative ideas alongside commercial, operational, and technical requirements.


Martin says: “We like to say internally we do constructable concepts. A client may have a really creative vision, and we want to help execute that. But we're also going, 'It doesn't fit your budget,' or 'It doesn't fit the ability to build this'.

“We spend that time telling that story, and we love doing it from a research lens with benchmarking, because a lot of clients will say, 'Oh, I want what this guy has.' Well, why do you want the same thing that he has?

"Let's come up with something more original, more creative, and now we're adding that level of story and theming and guest journey on top of it.”

Grap adds: “To me, this is one of the closest things to filmmaking, where all the disciplines come together, bringing the best in your field, and landing together on a project.”


Engineering can also inform the creative experience. Martin gives the example of an aquatic attraction designed around changes in water speed and movement.

"Our creatives have access to our smartest engineers. We have a guy on our team who does computational fluid dynamics modelling, and he’s brilliant at it. Our designers have ideas like, 'Hey, I want to do this with an action river,' and he'll work out a solution or a simulation and say, 'This is how you do it.'

“One of our team members spent months simulating a river as part of a creative story to tell the guest journey, with slow-down moments, speed-up moments, and waves being introduced.

“That is how we make engineering very much a part of the creative journey.”

This integration can also identify construction, budget and regulatory issues before a concept progresses too far.

Grap says: "That's the concept working with engineering to truly make it a reality versus putting something in front of a guest that might look pretty on a page but can't be delivered. It's that type of resource in the toolbox that elevates the entire project.”

See also: Blue Mar Wellness from Martin Aquatic

​Applying theme park thinking to water parks


Ectovox aims to bring theme park storytelling and environmental detail into water parks, creating different levels of engagement in the same space.

Grap says the approach starts with treating water park guests like theme park visitors.

"As a guest for years, I saw water parks not develop in tandem with theme parks; before working directly with Martin Aquatic, my approach was, 'I don't want to design a water park. I want to design a theme park with water-based attractions.'

“How do we make the space feel more lived in? How do we make it feel more active? Why can't we put this type of attraction in here just because it hasn't been done before? We really try to think of the environment as a whole, give it life and movement, and treat guests the same way you would a theme park guest."


“Some people just want the attractions; others want the story; and some want to know absolutely everything, and we want to satisfy all of them. We've said this for years: we're not designing for one visit; we're designing for your twentieth visit. The more we can add that enrichment and detail, the more enjoyable it's going to be across the board.

“Even if you're not paying attention to it, you're going to feel it.”

The philosophy is shaping Ectovox's work with Mattel, says Martin:

“With the work we're doing with Mattel right now, there are a lot of Easter eggs and hidden moments planned so that if you know the brands, we have something for you. When you look at it, we want to make sure we represent all those different moments, because guests notice different things.”


The team also uses visits to attractions and resorts as research, studying environmental detailing, show-set construction and guest movement. Martin calls these visits a ‘splash-about’:

"We look at some of the work we've done and orient new team members. When we say show set or dimensional flat, what do we actually mean? Looking at those items helps our team keep moving with that shared shorthand.

“What's great about our team across engineering and creative is that we have a bunch of really passionate people. We are very much bespoke creative every time.”

​Creating an African oasis at Hattiesburg Zoo


One of Ectovox’s early projects was Serengeti Springs, a water park expansion at Hattiesburg Zoo in Mississippi.

Martin Aquatic initially handled master planning and engineering, but as the project progressed, the zoo identified another need: a name, brand, and story for the new attraction.

Located alongside the zoo’s African animal habitats, the water park offered an opportunity to connect the two experiences. Ectovox helped develop it as an African oasis, giving the attraction its own identity while linking it to the surrounding zoo.


Martin says the team became involved late in the process.

"Serengeti Springs was a project where we did the master plan and design, and we were almost through full engineered documents when the client said, 'We don't have a name. What are we going to do?' I was in a meeting in Hattiesburg and said, 'Well, we have this division called Ectovox.'

“I introduced them, and two of our designers flew up to Mississippi and went through the guest journey and experience with that client to create a great logo and backstory. They had a great asset in their zoo, and the water park was adjacent to their Africa expansion, where you could literally look into their giraffe barn.

“They didn’t have the largest budget in the world, but they had so much passion and really wanted to put that extra level of detail into it.”


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Serengeti Springs at the Hattiesburg Zoo (@serengeti.springs)

Creative development extended beyond the name and logo. Ectovox worked with attraction supplier WhiteWater to adapt catalogue play structures to the theme.

Martin says: "The leadership in Hattiesburg told us, 'We want people to just forget that they're in Mississippi. How can I make Mississippi feel like an oasis where visitors can be completely transported?'

"Using that as a guide for the theme and name made it a really collaborative effort. What was great was how willing they were to take our concepts and run with them.”

Ectovox also produced a brand book and style guide, enabling the zoo to apply the identity across signage, merchandise and marketing.

​Translating Mattel's brands into aquatic experiences


Ectovox’s work with Mattel brings its approach to narrative and creative development into a branded indoor water park concept.

Mattel Wonder is planned as a series of permanent aquatic destinations built around the toy company’s brand portfolio. The first location, in Bellevue, Nebraska, is scheduled to open at the end of 2027.

The project involves more than translating familiar characters and products into a physical setting. The team must balance established brand guidelines with the technical demands of permanent aquatic environments, including chlorine, humidity, safety and maintenance.


Grap says the process involves helping established brands consider how their properties can work in a new environment.

"Working with a legacy brand that knows their brands one way, it's about helping them explore how these brands should and can exist in an entirely new environment. It's not as simple as a direct pull of just making that toy larger.

"It is about how guests want to engage with your brand versus how the brand may be perceived, and finding that middle ground.

“It's not just about scaling up; it's about the opportunity we can present. This isn't a temporary location that changes in a year; this is going to be here for decades, and we want to make sure we are delivering something that creates core memories for guests.”


Martin says the project also involves explaining the practical requirements of aquatic environments to the brand owners.

“Mattel and Hasbro are fantastic at making toys, but neither of them are water park or theme park operators at this stage in their companies. There's been an element of teaching what the guest will see, pointing out elements high up in the sky, and explaining what can actually survive in an aquatic environment.

“We have chlorine, splashes, safety regulations, and ASTM standards that you don't want to get in the way of creativity, but you have to make them aware of those elements. When you do permanent installations, you realise you're not going to change the slide colour in year two.”

The Bellevue project is also establishing a model that can be adapted for future Mattel Wonder locations. While the brand portfolio provides a common thread, Ectovox plans to vary the attraction mix, character groupings and spatial layouts.

Martin explains: "If you go to Nebraska, you get one great experience, but if you go to Illinois, you're going to have a Mattel Wonder park with a different collection of rides and toys to play with.”

​Developing original IP and new destinations


Licensed IP is only part of Ectovox's work. The studio also develops original characters and story worlds, offering an alternative when established IP doesn't fit a project's audience, location, or commercial strategy.

Martin says: "The team are so creative in what they're developing. Chris led a project to develop a full cast of original characters, and what they have created is so exciting.

“Too many people rely on licensing what they think crowds will flock to, when they could create an emotional attachment to something truly original and never before seen, or something local that represents a culture.

“Our team has that up its sleeve, speaking back to Chris's background with Mystery Cove, where there were original characters and storylines that guests could follow.”


Grap adds that developing original IP offers a different kind of creative challenge:

"Mall of America was like an incubator in that sense because I got to work with a ton of IP in various ways, but there is passion for both things. I love working with Mattel and Hasbro, but man, do I love the 'what if' of having a space to develop an original idea.

“There are so many ideas that we cycle through, and that moment of quiet celebration the team feels when an original idea we generated clicks with a client feels so good, even before a guest gets to see it.”

Ectovox is also applying its approach to cruise ships and integrated resorts, where the team must account for different technical constraints, including vessel stability, wind loads and high guest volumes.

For cruise projects, the aquatic experience forms part of a wider day rather than an isolated attraction.

Martin says: "Cruise lines typically don't invest in licensed IP; they want to create it and own the journey. When we approach design, I approach it as someone who's going to be on that ship and experience it. We're planning for an integrated water park resort or cruise ship from eight a.m. to midnight. How do we plan that entire day?

“Our aquatics and story are a key part of their journey, and understanding passenger behaviour helps tell that guest story.”

Recent projects include Norwegian Cruise Line's Great Stirrup Cay water park expansion, Great Tides, where the aquatic development forms part of the wider destination experience.

​Designing for long-term engagement


Ectovox is looking beyond traditional water parks, with work spanning dry theme parks, family entertainment centres, themed food and beverage, resort hotels and seasonal events.

The studio is developing original IP for resort environments, including room interiors, artwork, lobby storytelling and themed bar concepts. It is also exploring how attractions can accommodate different uses throughout the year.

Planning seasonal overlays and after-dark events from the outset lets operators incorporate lighting infrastructure, sound systems, and prop anchor points into the master plan, reducing the need for major retrofits.


Grap argues that digital tools should support the physical experience rather than become the experience itself.

"There's too much reliance on trying to push tech into the park. I want people to forget their devices—make it optional to opt in, but not everything needs to go back to your cell phone.

“For years, water parks were concrete jungles with a bunch of columns and fibreglass where you didn't see much of what was happening. We're working hard to consider how guests approach certain things, giving them exciting engagement as early as possible to create a sense of life and a reason for everything.

“It's less reliance on tech, more reliance on what's happening in real life, and being intentional with it.”

For Ectovox, creative development extends beyond opening day to how destinations evolve.

Martin says:

"We want Ectovox to continue to expand beyond just the aquatic space into dry parks and facilities. Beyond that, it will be seasonal overlays and ongoing programming—what do you do with your water park after dark, or in the cold, or for Halloween and Christmas overlays? If you don't plan it on day one, it's hard to execute later.

“Our goal is to be involved with our clients for the long term, setting up that schedule, and helping them build lasting, story-driven destinations.”

title: ​Chance Rides at 65: innovation, experience and the next generation of attractions
summary:
For 65 years, Chance Rides has adapted familiar attraction formats to changing technology, markets and guest expectations. Now, as the company marks a milestone anniversary, that history provides a lens on what might shape the next 65 years.

Founded in 1961 by Harold Chance, the company began with the CP Huntington train, which would become one of its signature offerings.


Over the decades, Chance expanded into portable rides, carousels, roller coasters, people movers, observation wheels and other attractions. Its engineering and manufacturing capabilities evolved alongside that expanding portfolio.

Today, its products serve a wide range of markets and customer types, from theme parks, family entertainment centres, zoos and aquariums to travelling operators.

It is an approach Chance sees continuing into the next generation of attractions: using technology to improve the product and the experience without losing sight of the people who ultimately ride it.

​A culture of innovation


President and CEO Aaron Landrum identifies the development of the CP Huntington as a defining moment in Chance's history. The next major shift came with portability.

“That was a fundamental shift when, at that time, the industry was taking days or weeks to set up a ride. Now it got down to a day or two. Chance really was at the forefront of that evolution of portability for showmen.”


Portability changed the commercial possibilities for travelling operators, while also establishing a pattern that would recur throughout Chance's history: applying its engineering and manufacturing capabilities to new markets.

“In the 80s, we got into the carousel business, a whole new product line. In the 90s, we started developing people movers, trams. Then we got into observation wheels.”

The company's development continued into the 2000s, including the acquisition of D.H. Morgan, while more recent years have brought international partnerships, including with EVX Mobility in Sweden.

Along the way, individual products marked important steps in that evolution, from the trailer-mounted Trabant to the Superman coaster built for Six Flags Mexico.

“That culture of constant innovation was a defining feature over 65 years.”

The result is a portfolio that spans very different attraction formats, but shares a common foundation in engineering, manufacturing and long-term product development.

​Engineering the ride before it is built


The technology behind that development has changed significantly.

Jeremy McClanahan, operations manager at Chance Rides, says the move from traditional two-dimensional drawings to three-dimensional engineering has transformed the design process.

“That transition has allowed us to simulate, validate, and refine our designs long before the first parts are produced.”

Manufacturing has evolved alongside engineering, with CNC equipment, improved fabrication processes, and greater automation improving consistency and quality.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Chance Rides, LLC (@chanceridesllc)

However, for Travis Lane, project management director, these technologies matter for more than producing a more precise piece of machinery. They change how much of the design work can happen before manufacturing begins.

“A lot of it now is upfront. It's anticipatory,” he says. “When you have those powerful modelling tools and software that allow you to make a rapid change, as opposed to, hey, we are committed to this print, or even we're committed to this delivery date, and we have to release a ride right now.”

That upfront process creates more opportunities to iterate. It is also increasingly important as expectations around safety, reliability and regulatory compliance become more demanding.

Technology may have transformed the process, but McClanahan stresses that manufacturing fundamentals have not disappeared.

“There's still a high level of craftsmanship that goes into each ride that we build…technology has enhanced craftsmanship, not replaced it.”

​Designing around the guest


Some of the biggest changes are not technological. They concern who attractions are being designed for.

Chance has seen a shift away from designing primarily around individual age demographics toward experiences that accommodate wider groups and multigenerational families, Landrum explains.

“Now it's more about the whole family. How do you get the really small kids and all the way to grandpa in there?”

That has implications for ride design, accessibility and the overall experience.

Chance also considers guests with different physical abilities, sensory sensitivities, and other needs in the design process.

“How do we make a ride or an attraction or experience something the whole family can enjoy?” Landrum asks.

That can mean considering how an experience responds to guests who experience sensory overload, for example, and whether elements can be adjusted.


At the same time, operators are asking for increasingly ambitious creative experiences.

That creates a more complex design brief: attractions need to deliver creative impact while accommodating a broader range of guests and meeting technical and regulatory requirements.

One example is the psychedelic Looper carousel created for Area15 in Las Vegas. The underlying attraction format was familiar, but the creative treatment represented a different direction for Chance.

“From a design philosophy perspective, the level of creative design and free-thinking artistic approach that we took to that signalled that the company is ready and willing to go in creative directions that it may not have been 30 years ago.”

​Listening to operators


One of Chance's most important sources of innovation isn't a new piece of technology. It is conversation. Landrum describes operator feedback as “the most fundamental thing that we can have – the voice of the customer.”

Operators are interacting with guests every day. They see how people behave in queues, how they respond to attractions and where operational problems arise. “They are talking to guests constantly. They're watching. They're observing. They're listening.

“It could be as simple as, ‘We’d like to have this restraint a little bit easier to work with,’ or it could be ‘We really want a more immersive experience on the carousel’.”


Chance therefore asks operators directly, he adds: “What's going well? What do you want different? What do you need different? What are your dreams?"

Landrum says the company avoids assuming it already knows what operators want.

“We've got to take the blinders off of what we're trying to accomplish, and that direct engagement of listening to the operators is probably the most fundamental thing we have to do to make sure that we hear them and we respond to what their needs are, and don't preconceive what we believe they want.”

In other words: “We build and design what they desire.”

​Building for the long term


That relationship extends beyond product development. Chance describes customers as partners through installation, operation, maintenance and refurbishment. “It's a marriage,” says Landrum.

That relationship matters because attractions are significant capital investments, and their value depends on how effectively they perform over many years.

McClanahan adds: “We were a family-owned business. I think family is important. Teamwork is big. We all work together to solve any problem or challenge that we come across. And we always come through for the customer.”

That support becomes particularly important when operators assess a ride's whole-life economics.


“The customer wants to be taken care of too,” McClanahan says. “After the sale, after the installation, they want somebody that's going to be there for them. If they call, they want to know somebody's going to answer.”

Landrum puts it simply: “They're never alone when they buy a product from Chance. We're always here for them.”

Yet the appeal of a ride has to be matched by a viable business case.

Chance is seeing increasing focus on throughput, reliability, maintenance, repeatability and total cost of ownership.

Landrum says operators are asking questions such as: “What does it cost me to operate this on a daily basis? What's my throughput? So, what's my return on investment on a guest per hour or guest per day?”

They are also considering how a ride contributes to the wider destination. For a carousel, for example, that could mean drawing guests into an area for food and beverage, telling a story or supporting a wider destination proposition.

​Reliability with Chance Rides


An attraction's longevity is another part of the equation. Landrum says this is where Chance sees much of its value proposition.

“You buy a Chance product, and you take good care of it; it'll be in your park for 30 years. And we can retheme it; we can make it look like something different.”

That makes an attraction's value a question not only of opening-day performance, but of how much life and flexibility you can build into the asset.

Reliability is central to that calculation.


Lane notes that “99% is no longer a good enough uptime” when operators are building business cases around attraction performance. “All of the calculations on paper, it all divides by zero if the ride is down.”

That makes maintainability and reliability considerations that need to be built into a project from the beginning.

“Ultimately, you have to build right, and you have to build in a way that somebody can get their hands in it and make those maintenance updates and swap things out if needed and keep the ride up.”

That flexibility also has to work across markets. Chance works with different regulatory frameworks and cultural expectations, which can affect everything from restraint procedures to how ride attendants interact with guests.

Landrum gives the example of personal space:

“How does a ride operator, that person, work in the line? How do I check a restraint while respecting a person's personal space and cultural norms?”

Chance says the answer is to ask, not assume.

“That's the openness; we are open to saying, ‘We don't know this, but let's talk to people who do, and understand how we can bridge that.'”

​Physical experiences in a digital world


Landrum describes a renewed appetite for shared physical experiences following the pandemic.

Before COVID, he says, there was considerable enthusiasm around digitisation, virtual reality and increasingly individualised experiences. Since then, he says, the value of experiences that bring people together has become more apparent.

“The industry wants experiences the whole family can enjoy.”

He adds: “While virtual reality, artificial intelligence, and other digital aspects of our experiences are important, there's still that physical experience; feeling the accelerations, feeling the wind in your face, feeling something that's different.”


The Chance team believes the opportunity is not to choose between technology and physical attractions, but to use technology where it enhances the overall experience, he continues:

“How do we tell a story? How does it pull everyone in and keep people engaged within a park or a zoo or whatever the destination might be?”

Lane sees another factor at play: the growing accessibility of digital experiences at home.

“If you can get a VR headset at home, well, you probably aren't going to have a carousel at home, so that becomes the novel experience that then makes you go out.

“One of the things that I enjoy about Chance is that a lot of our products and services are really timeless.”

Demand may fluctuate, he says, but some motivations remain.

“There are appealing things that are always going to be there. You want to go on something fast. Or you want to ride something with your family. There's always a joy to that.”

​Looking beyond the ride


Sustainability is another area where Chance sees technology connecting environmental considerations with commercial realities. Recent work includes electrifying the CP Huntington and launching the eTRAM electric people mover.

Landrum says the company is also considering how attractions can have longer and more useful lifecycles, including repairability and replaceable subassemblies.

“When it comes to sustainability, it's not just about doing what's right for us as a species, but it's also about return on investment. Take care of your product; it will last.”

Lane sees this as an increasingly practical argument for sustainable technology. “Sometimes you do it because it's the right thing, and sometimes you do it because it makes financial or economic or technological sense.”

An electric, solar-powered people mover, for example, can have environmental benefits while also offering operational advantages.


He also points to potentially lower maintenance requirements. “It's got fewer moving parts to maintain. It's got fewer things that can break.”

That puts sustainability alongside more familiar questions around maintenance, reliability, operating cost and asset life.

Storytelling and immersion are another area of opportunity. Landrum points to the potential for attractions that do more than deliver a physical thrill. “How do I tell a story?” For zoos and aquariums in particular, he sees opportunities to use familiar attraction formats to deliver education and conservation messaging.

“How do we take a carousel and turn that into a way to tell a story about conservation, or hey, this is the life cycle of this animal, or this is fauna that's in your area?”

The aim is to give guests something beyond the physical experience.

Technology is part of the opportunity, but Chance sees it as a means, not the experience itself.

Landrum says AI is a tool that can support creative teams rather than replace them. “It can support that innovation. But you cannot take a human element out.”


McClanahan adds that the challenge is to bring those emerging technologies together while retaining the craftsmanship that underpins the company's products. “It's about tying all that technology together, but yet still putting out that craftsmanship into what we build.”

Technology could also have a practical role in attraction operations. McClanahan sees opportunities for more interactive diagnostic and maintenance systems that could guide technicians through troubleshooting and make technical information more accessible.

“One of the big things that we can do is make that equipment, from a maintenance standpoint or from an operator standpoint, more interactive, so that the operator or the maintenance tech can walk through how to do what they need to do.”

That points to a broader role for manufacturers: not simply supplying equipment, but helping operators manage the attraction throughout its working life.

​The next 65 years


Chance's vision for the next 65 years rests on many of the same principles that shaped its first 65: adaptation, engineering, and a focus on the experience itself.

Landrum does not expect the company's fundamental purpose to change.

“We are and will continue to be known for safe, reliable products. You need somebody to help you and work with you and not just be an equipment manufacturer. That's going to be Chance.

“We're a species that desires experiences. We want to feel something, and I think Chance at 65 is going to help feed that feeling of experiences and memories.”


For McClanahan, the foundation is similarly straightforward.

“At the end of the day, we're a business of creating experiences that bring people together. It's easy to focus on the technical side of what we build, but behind everything we do, from design reviews to the meetings that we have, ultimately it puts a smile on a person's face. It brings people together.”

Lane returns to the company's existing motto, “Joy in Motion”, and argues that it remains as relevant to the future as it has been to the past.

“If I had the power to change that, I don't think I would. I think that's exactly the right DNA for the company.”

He adds the enduring appeal of attractions comes down to something simple: "There's something fundamental about being able to participate in a kid getting on a ride and having their eyes light up with that joy.”

Technology will change the shape of attractions. Creative design will evolve. New products will emerge, and established products will be reinvented.

“But somebody's always going to want to get on a ride, and somebody's got to build that ride and design that ride.”

“How do we take a carousel and turn that into a way to tell a story about conservation, or hey, this is the life cycle of this animal, or this is fauna that's in your area?”

The aim is to give guests something beyond the physical experience.

Technology is part of the opportunity, but Chance sees it as a means, not the experience itself.

Landrum says AI is a tool that can support creative teams rather than replace them. “It can support that innovation. But you cannot take a human element out.”


McClanahan adds that the challenge is to bring those emerging technologies together while retaining the craftsmanship that underpins the company's products. “It's about tying all that technology together, but yet still putting out that craftsmanship into what we build.”

Technology could also have a practical role in attraction operations. McClanahan sees opportunities for more interactive diagnostic and maintenance systems that could guide technicians through troubleshooting and make technical information more accessible.

“One of the big things that we can do is make that equipment, from a maintenance standpoint or from an operator standpoint, more interactive, so that the operator or the maintenance tech can walk through how to do what they need to do.”

That points to a broader role for manufacturers: not simply supplying equipment, but helping operators manage the attraction throughout its working life.

​The next 65 years


Chance's vision for the next 65 years rests on many of the same principles that shaped its first 65: adaptation, engineering, and a focus on the experience itself.

Landrum does not expect the company's fundamental purpose to change.

“We are and will continue to be known for safe, reliable products. You need somebody to help you and work with you and not just be an equipment manufacturer. That's going to be Chance.

“We're a species that desires experiences. We want to feel something, and I think Chance at 65 is going to help feed that feeling of experiences and memories.”


For McClanahan, the foundation is similarly straightforward.

“At the end of the day, we're a business of creating experiences that bring people together. It's easy to focus on the technical side of what we build, but behind everything we do, from design reviews to the meetings that we have, ultimately it puts a smile on a person's face. It brings people together.”

Lane returns to the company's existing motto, “Joy in Motion”, and argues that it remains as relevant to the future as it has been to the past.

“If I had the power to change that, I don't think I would. I think that's exactly the right DNA for the company.”

He adds the enduring appeal of attractions comes down to something simple: "There's something fundamental about being able to participate in a kid getting on a ride and having their eyes light up with that joy.”

Technology will change the shape of attractions. Creative design will evolve. New products will emerge, and established products will be reinvented.

“But somebody's always going to want to get on a ride, and somebody's got to build that ride and design that ride.”

title: Tokyo Disneyland sets opening date for new 'Wreck-It Ralph' ride
summary:
Tokyo Disneyland has set an opening date for its new Wreck-It Ralph ride, Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue.

The world’s first Wreck-It Ralph-themed attraction will officially open on 15 April, 2027 at Tokyo Disneyland, coinciding with the theme park's 44th anniversary.

A redesign of the park's former Buzz Lightyear interactive dark ride, Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue invites guests on an adventure alongside Ralph and Vanellope to defeat King Candy.

Tokyo Disneyland’s new Pixel Prism shop will feature pixel-patterned flooring, fibre optic-inspired designs and attraction merchandiseDisney

In the new attraction, King Candy is plotting to take over the world of video games and has transformed the candies of Sugar Rush into Sugar Bugs programmed to consume the whole kingdom.

On the new ride, guests will enter the Sugar Rush game world from the Wreck-It Ralph films, teaming up with Ralph and Vanellope to restore the Sugar Bugs to their original kawaii forms before they destroy everything.

The ride will let guests scan the bugs using devices onboard ride vehicles, transforming them back to their original forms. Points will be awarded based on the types and number of Sugar Bugs restored.

Riders will be able to view their results on the ride vehicle screens and, for a limited time, in the Tokyo Disney Resort app, where ride photos will also be available to purchase.

Tokyo Disneyland’s Tomorrowland expansion includes Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue, Space Mountain Earthrise and new shopping and dining optionsDisney

Outside the ride, Pixel Prism, a new shop selling Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue merchandise, will also open on 15 April 2027.

Popping Station, a new popcorn stand overlooking Tomorrowland Plaza, will open on 17 March, serving Sugar-Lime Popcorn inspired by the attraction.

Ahead of the attraction’s opening, a Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue-inspired smartphone mini-game will launch on 12 January, followed by themed decorations and photo opportunities in Tomorrowland in February and Cinderella Castle projections in March.

Sugar Rush: Sweet Rescue will join the new Space Mountain Earthrise indoor roller coaster, also opening in 2027, as part of a 100 billion yen ($630 million) transformation of Tokyo Disneyland’s Tomorrowland.
